paragraphs: Sampling from a heavy-tailed distribution requires representing outcomes far from its center as well as typical ones. This paper studies how the choice of oracle within a proximal sampler affects the computational effort needed to achieve a specified accuracy. Accuracy is measured using chi-squared divergence between the sampler’s output distribution and its target.

The authors establish a separation between Gaussian and stable oracles. For a class of heavy-tailed targets, Gaussian-oracle proximal samplers necessarily need at least polynomially many iterations in the inverse error tolerance. Stable-oracle proximal samplers can instead achieve a logarithmic dependence. This distinction becomes especially consequential when the requested error is very small: tightening accuracy can increase the required work at fundamentally different rates.

The paper also proves lower bounds for stable-oracle samplers, showing that its upper bounds cannot be fundamentally improved. The contribution therefore identifies both a barrier for one sampler family and a theoretically supported way past it, within the heavy-tailed sampling setting studied.
neurips-2024-a-separation-in-heavy-taile.tldr: Stable-oracle proximal samplers achieve high-accuracy guarantees that Gaussian-oracle samplers cannot match for a class of heavy-tailed targets.

paragraphs: General Value Functions express predictive knowledge by estimating the expected return associated with a policy and a particular reward signal. Learning several of these predictions together can make poor use of data when experience comes from a fixed behavior policy or an existing dataset. The policy collecting observations may not gather the experience most useful for all the predictions being learned.

GVFExplorer learns one adaptive behavior policy to collect data for multiple value functions in parallel. It adjusts that policy to minimize total return variance across the predictions, using an existing temporal-difference-style estimator to approximate the variance. This makes exploration responsive to the combined evaluation problem, with the aim of reducing the environmental interactions needed.

The authors prove that each behavior-policy update decreases overall mean squared prediction error in their analysis. Experiments cover tabular representations and nonlinear function approximation, including Mujoco environments and both stationary and changing reward signals. The reported findings support improved data use and reduced prediction errors across multiple value functions.
neurips-2024-adaptive-exploration-for-da.tldr: GVFExplorer adapts a shared exploration policy to reduce prediction error and data requirements when evaluating multiple general value functions.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much of a strong chess engine’s planning ability a transformer can absorb through supervised learning. The authors introduce ChessBench, containing 10 million games and 15 billion annotated data points, with legal moves and values supplied by Stockfish 16. Chess provides a test of generalization to novel positions where memorization alone is insufficient.

They train transformers with up to 270 million parameters and examine dataset size, model size, architecture, and prediction targets. Those targets include position values, action values, and direct imitation of moves. Predicting action values allows a learned model to capture judgments produced by a search-based engine without performing explicit search when choosing its own moves.

The largest models predict action values accurately on unfamiliar boards. The resulting policy solves difficult chess puzzles and reaches a Lichess blitz Elo of 2895 against humans, described as grandmaster level. However, the authors also find that distillation remains imperfect. The results demonstrate substantial transferred planning capability while leaving room to improve how faithfully transformers reproduce the teacher’s decisions.
neurips-2024-amortized-planning-with-lar.tldr: Transformers trained on Stockfish annotations achieve grandmaster-level chess performance without explicit search, although they do not perfectly reproduce the engine.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial decisions must be made before their relevant costs or other parameters are known. A prediction model estimates these quantities, and an optimization solver uses them to select a decision. Predict-then-Optimize trains the predictor with a supervised objective, whereas Predict-and-Optimize trains toward the quality of the final decision.

This paper creates a modular benchmark for comparing these approaches and their component choices. It evaluates 11 existing methods on eight problems and introduces an industrial dataset for combinatorial advertising. The framework brings representative applications and a categorization of existing methods into one setting, making comparisons across pipeline designs more systematic.

Predict-and-Optimize performs better than Predict-then-Optimize on seven of the eight benchmarks. However, the study finds no universally best set of design choices within Predict-and-Optimize. These findings support training for decision quality in many evaluated settings while showing that the particular implementation still matters. The framework also supports rapid prototyping for applications and provides a common basis for developing future methods.
neurips-2024-benchmarking-pto-and-pno-me.tldr: A benchmark of 11 predictive optimization methods finds that decision-focused training wins on seven of eight problems, without a universally best design.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents usually learn from rewards they observe after acting. Sparse rewards already make exploration difficult, but a further complication arises when some rewards cannot be observed at all. The paper examines this distinction in settings connected to partial monitoring and monitored Markov decision processes.

A common exploration principle is optimism: favor possibilities that might turn out well while uncertainty remains. The authors explain that this principle can produce suboptimal behavior when rewards are sometimes hidden. An optimistic agent may fail to take the additional exploratory actions needed to resolve its uncertainty, leaving it without the information required to improve its decisions.

The paper proposes an exploration strategy that addresses this failure and establishes convergence to an optimal policy in the setting studied, even with intermittently unobservable rewards. It also introduces tabular benchmark environments covering both observable and unobservable rewards. Reported comparisons show the proposed method outperforming existing approaches, supporting the value of exploration strategies that explicitly address whether reward information can be acquired.
neurips-2024-beyond-optimism-exploration.tldr: A new exploration strategy addresses failures of optimism when rewards are sometimes unobservable and guarantees convergence in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Estimating a joint probability density becomes difficult as the number of variables grows. Without structural assumptions, the required data can suffer from the curse of dimensionality. This paper studies densities whose conditional independence relationships obey the Markov conditions of an undirected graph, using that structure to characterize the difficulty of estimation.

The central contribution is a graph quantity called graph resilience. The authors show that it determines the optimal sample complexity of the structured estimation problem, with results applying to arbitrary graphs. This differs from an explanation based only on sparsity, manifold structure, or local graph properties. In particular, quantities such as node degree do not by themselves describe the relevant sample-complexity behavior.

The paper derives uniform deviation bounds for explicit examples and shows how graph structure can avoid or substantially lessen dimensionality-related difficulty. Sequential, hierarchical, and spatial data provide notable cases with improved rates. The result ties the possible statistical benefit to the assumed Markov structure rather than promising the same improvement for every high-dimensional distribution.
neurips-2024-breaking-the-curse-of-dimen.tldr: Graph resilience characterizes optimal sample complexity for graph-structured density estimation and explains when dimensionality-related difficulty can be reduced.

paragraphs: Rare transitions are difficult to sample because ordinary simulation can spend substantial effort producing trajectories that never reach the event of interest. For Brownian dynamics with known drift, Doob’s h-transform describes how to condition a process on reaching a chosen endpoint or rare event. Directly estimating that transform is nevertheless computationally impractical when it requires enough forward simulations to measure tiny event probabilities.

The authors reformulate the transform as a variational optimization problem over trajectories connecting specified starting and ending points. They introduce a simulation-free training objective and a model representation that satisfies the endpoint requirements by construction. Building these conditions into the model reduces the trajectory search space.

The approach avoids the expensive trajectory simulations and inefficient importance-sampling estimators required by existing methods discussed in the paper. Demonstrations on molecular simulation and protein-folding tasks show that it can find feasible transition paths. The contribution is a computational route to conditioned dynamics within the stated known-drift setting, supported by examples involving physically meaningful rare transitions.
neurips-2024-doob-s-lagrangian-a-sample-.tldr: A variational formulation of Doob’s h-transform enables simulation-free training for finding rare transition paths with built-in endpoint constraints.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction turns point predictions into intervals with valid coverage under standard assumptions. Full conformal prediction can be expensive because it considers candidate labels across the possible output space and repeatedly trains the estimator. Existing acceleration methods often impose strong assumptions, apply only to particular models, or provide approximate prediction sets.

This paper develops a framework for fast exact conformalization across generalized statistical estimation problems. Its analysis follows how the fitted solution changes as the candidate label varies. The authors establish that this solution path is piecewise smooth and show that second-order information from difference equations is sufficient to approximate the full range of solutions to arbitrary accuracy.

That structure provides a way to organize the computation around a connected solution path. The framework offers a unified interpretation of earlier work, adds geometric insight, and integrates with established numerical solvers. Experiments across numerous benchmarks demonstrate substantial speedups over standard methods. The intended benefit is to make full conformal procedures more practical while retaining the exact-conformalization objective.
neurips-2024-generalized-fast-exact-conf.tldr: Piecewise-smooth solution paths enable a general framework for accelerating exact conformalization, with substantial benchmark speedups.

paragraphs: Federated learning must train a shared model from clients whose local data can differ substantially. The problem becomes harder when communication limits allow only a small fraction of clients to participate in each round. Choosing which clients contribute therefore affects both training progress and the computational cost of organizing that training.

HiCS-FL uses updates to the network’s output layer to estimate statistical differences among clients’ datasets. The server uses these estimates to cluster clients and guide sampling. This connects client selection to information already expressed through model updates, addressing the overhead and restricted heterogeneity patterns associated with existing selection approaches.

The authors analyze how well their techniques compare dataset heterogeneity and characterize convergence when the selection method is used for training. Extensive experiments in non-identically distributed settings report faster convergence than state-of-the-art client-selection schemes and a substantial reduction in selection computation. The findings also indicate adaptability across different heterogeneity scenarios, supporting the method as a way to make limited client participation more effective.
neurips-2024-heterogeneity-guided-client.tldr: HiCS-FL uses output-layer updates to guide client clustering and sampling, improving convergence and reducing selection costs in heterogeneous federated learning.

paragraphs: A classifier is calibrated when its confidence scores align with its accuracy. Dataset shifts can disrupt that alignment, but measuring the problem in a new domain often requires labels that are unavailable. This paper addresses calibration under label shift, where class frequencies change while the distribution of inputs within each class stays the same.

The authors introduce a consistent estimator of calibration error that does not require target-domain labels. Its stated consistency is tied to the label-shift setting. This fills a gap between estimators that need labeled target examples and estimators built around a different assumption, covariate shift.

LaSCal combines this estimator with a post-hoc calibration strategy to adjust confidence on the target distribution without target labels. The estimator supplies a way to assess confidence alignment, and the calibration step uses that information to improve it. Empirical evaluations across modalities, model architectures, and shift intensities support the approach’s effectiveness and reliability. The central benefit is making target-domain calibration possible under the specified distributional change.
neurips-2024-lascal-label-shift-calibrat.tldr: LaSCal estimates calibration error and recalibrates predictions without target labels under a label-shift assumption.

paragraphs: Masked prediction trains a model to infer hidden portions of its input. In offline reinforcement learning, different masking patterns can support several downstream decision-making tasks within a single pretrained model. However, that flexibility leaves a training question: how should the model balance skills that differ in complexity?

CurrMask addresses this by changing the masking scheme during pretraining. The masks form a curriculum that adjusts the prediction problems the model encounters as learning proceeds. The approach therefore makes the organization of pretraining tasks part of the learning method, with the goal of building a versatile collection of decision-making skills.

Experiments report superior zero-shot performance on skill-prompting and goal-conditioned planning tasks, along with competitive performance after finetuning on offline reinforcement learning tasks. Analysis of the training dynamics indicates that the changing masks accompany gradual acquisition of skills at different complexity levels. These results connect the curriculum mechanism to both the development of skills during training and their usefulness across the evaluated downstream tasks.
neurips-2024-learning-versatile-skills-w.tldr: CurrMask adapts masking patterns during pretraining to build skills of varying complexity and improve zero-shot decision-making performance.

paragraphs: Zero-shot audio classifiers make decisions using relationships between sounds and text descriptions. Explaining those decisions requires preserving what the classifier finds relevant to the supplied text. This paper introduces LMAC-ZS, a post-hoc method that uses a decoder to produce explanations that can be listened to.

The central design is a loss function intended to reproduce the original similarity patterns between audio and text pairs. This gives the explanation process a direct connection to the classifier’s decision mechanism: the generated explanation should retain the relationships that made particular descriptions match the original audio. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first decoder-based post-hoc explanation method for zero-shot audio classification.

An extensive evaluation with the CLAP model supports the interpreter’s faithfulness to classification decisions in the zero-shot setting. Qualitative results also show meaningful explanations that correspond well to different text prompts. Together, these findings support listenable explanations as a way to inspect both a model’s audio decisions and their dependence on the accompanying language.
neurips-2024-listenable-maps-for-zero-sh.tldr: LMAC-ZS generates listenable explanations that aim to preserve the text–audio similarity patterns behind zero-shot audio classifications.

paragraphs: Learning dynamics from images requires connecting visible motion to the process producing it. Purely neural simulators can violate physical laws, while traditional simulators depend on expert-written equations that may not capture actual behavior completely. NeuMA combines existing physical laws with learned corrections to better fit observed dynamics.

The physical component supplies interpretable prior structure, and the learned adaptor accounts for behavior that this structure does not fully represent. To connect the simulator with images, the authors introduce Particle-GS, a particle-driven variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It allows image gradients to flow back into the simulator, making visual observations usable for optimizing its dynamics.

Experiments examine several kinds of dynamics through particle accuracy, dynamic rendering quality, and generalization ability. The reported results show that NeuMA can capture intrinsic dynamics accurately while retaining the generalizability and interpretability associated with physical priors. The contribution combines a hybrid dynamics model with a visual connection that lets image evidence directly guide the learning of that model.
neurips-2024-neuma-neural-material-adapt.tldr: NeuMA combines physical laws with learned corrections and a differentiable image representation to learn dynamics from visual observations.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes geometric organization of learned features and classifier weights near the end of training. For imbalanced data, imposing an optimal geometry can reduce minority collapse without matching established methods that learn their classifiers. This paper asks whether a different geometry can encode a better classification rule.

The authors justify assigning minority classes more directions, called centers, and derive a Generalized Classification Rule from this idea. Under an MSE-type loss in the Unconstrained Features Model, they show that features from a class tend to collapse to the mean of its assigned centers at the global optimum. When this occurs, the original classifier approximates a surrogate for the proposed rule.

They use the analysis to develop a strategy for choosing center counts and a Cosine Loss for a fixed classifier. Experiments show that this loss can induce the proposed multiple-center collapse and achieve long-tail classification performance comparable to classical imbalance-learning methods. The work links a specific feature geometry to a practical classification strategy.
neurips-2024-neural-collapse-to-multiple.tldr: Assigning multiple centers to classes yields a new collapse geometry and a fixed-classifier training method competitive on long-tail classification.

paragraphs: Convolutional residual networks can predict well even when they have far more parameters than conventional intuition would suggest is necessary. This paper studies that behavior through nonparametric classification theory. It analyzes ConvResNeXts trained with weight decay, a network family that includes convolutional residual networks as a special case.

The theoretical framework allows infinitely many building blocks and shows that weight decay implicitly encourages sparsity among them. Thus, an extremely large available architecture can still have a sparse effective organization. This provides a mechanism connecting regularized training with control over how much of the architecture is used.

The main learning result assumes a smooth target function supported on a low-dimensional manifold. Under that structure, the authors prove that ConvResNeXts can adapt to both function smoothness and low-dimensional geometry, learning efficiently without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. The result offers a partial theoretical justification for the advantages of overparameterized networks, with the explanation specifically grounded in the stated target-function structure and regularization.
neurips-2024-nonparametric-classificatio.tldr: Under smoothness and low-dimensional manifold assumptions, weight-decayed ConvResNeXts adapt efficiently while implicitly selecting a sparse set of blocks.

paragraphs: Connected nodes do not always have similar features. This feature heterophily can matter when a graph neural network predicts links, but much prior understanding of heterophily concerns node classification and class labels. The paper studies link prediction directly, where such labels are unavailable and the relevant question is whether two nodes should be connected.

The authors formally define homophilic and heterophilic link-prediction tasks and develop a theoretical framework showing that they call for different optimization behavior. They then examine how encoders and decoders respond to varying feature similarity and propose improved designs. This separates the roles of constructing node representations and converting those representations into link predictions.

The evaluation includes synthetic data and six real-world benchmarks spanning different similarity regimes, with graphs containing up to 30 million edges. Results support the theoretical insights and emphasize learnable decoders together with message-passing encoders that keep a node’s own embedding separate from its neighbors’ embeddings. These design choices matter when link prediction extends beyond connections between similar nodes.
neurips-2024-on-the-impact-of-feature-he.tldr: Theory and experiments show why link prediction between dissimilar nodes benefits from learnable decoders and separate self and neighbor representations.

paragraphs: A single-index model assumes that a linear combination of predictors contains the information needed to relate them to the response. This offers flexibility and interpretability, but outliers and heavy-tailed errors can undermine estimation efficiency. The paper develops a robust inference procedure for this model when the number of predictors is high.

The method transforms the responses and recasts the problem as a pseudo-linear model. This permits more general error distributions than the sub-Gaussian conditions used in less robust formulations. Within this framework, orthogonalization supports inference about groups of coefficients without requiring zero and nonzero coefficients to be clearly separated.

The authors establish asymptotically honest group inference, derive the null distribution, and provide a bootstrap implementation. They also introduce simultaneous testing of individual coefficients with asymptotic false discovery rate control. These guarantees concern large-sample behavior. Numerical results indicate that the procedures can compete strongly with existing methods, especially under heavy-tailed errors, connecting the relaxed error assumptions to useful gains in robust statistical inference.
neurips-2024-robust-group-and-simultaneo.tldr: A transformed-response approach enables robust group inference and simultaneous coefficient testing for high-dimensional single-index models with more general errors.

paragraphs: Expert demonstrations may reflect contextual information that the learner never observes. Consequently, experts can appear to solve the same decision problem while actually responding to related but different tasks. This paper studies how to use such demonstrations for online sequential decision-making when the hidden task distribution is also unknown.

The authors formulate the problem as zero-shot meta-reinforcement learning with a Bayesian regret objective. Hidden tasks are represented by parameters with an unknown prior. Their ExPerior algorithm uses empirical Bayes to infer an informative prior from expert data. That prior can then support Bayesian online decision-making methods, including posterior sampling.

This approach uses demonstrations to shape the learner’s initial beliefs about its decision problem while allowing subsequent online learning. Evaluations span multi-armed bandits, Markov decision processes, and partially observable Markov decision processes. The reported results outperform behavior cloning, online algorithms, and online-offline baselines in these settings. They support extracting useful prior information from expert behavior even when the context behind that behavior is not recorded.
neurips-2024-sequential-decision-making-.tldr: ExPerior turns demonstrations shaped by hidden expert context into an informative prior for Bayesian online decision-making.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models can accept human skeletons as pose guidance, but complex configurations remain difficult, particularly side and rear views. Stable-Pose introduces an adapter for pretrained Stable Diffusion that improves how a supplied pose guides image synthesis. Its main mechanism is a vision transformer with attention masks refined from coarse to fine.

The transformer’s query-key self-attention captures relationships among anatomical parts in the skeleton. Masked pose images guide hierarchical refinement of attention maps toward features relevant to the requested pose. A complementary loss gives additional emphasis to the pose region, directing training toward accurate representation of intricate body configurations.

The authors evaluate Stable-Pose on five public datasets covering indoor and outdoor human poses. On LAION-Human, it achieves an AP score of 57.1, reported as roughly a 13 percent improvement over ControlNet. These findings support the usefulness of progressively refined pose attention and region-focused training for the evaluated generation tasks, including conditions where skeleton guidance is difficult for existing methods.
neurips-2024-stable-pose-leveraging-tran.tldr: Stable-Pose improves skeleton-guided image generation using progressively refined transformer attention and a loss emphasizing pose regions.

paragraphs: Learning differential equations from observed motion can involve searching through many candidate expressions. If the search ignores physical symmetries such as frame invariance, it may consider unnecessary candidates and return equations that are overly complicated or inaccurate. This paper uses symmetry to restrict the search for governing equations.

The authors derive equivariance constraints from time-independent symmetries of ordinary differential equations. These constraints express how an equation should behave under the relevant transformations. They develop a pipeline that incorporates the constraints into different discovery algorithms, including sparse regression and genetic programming, with the integration depending on the type of symmetry.

The approach matters because it uses physical structure to narrow the candidate space while pursuing simpler and more accurate equations. Experiments across diverse dynamical systems show stronger robustness to noise and a significantly higher probability of recovering the governing equations than baselines that omit symmetry. The findings support symmetry information as a useful ingredient in automated discovery across the tested systems and algorithm families.
neurips-2024-symmetry-informed-governing.tldr: Constraints derived from time-independent symmetries narrow equation-discovery searches and improve recovery and noise robustness in experiments.

paragraphs: Differential privacy restricts how much an algorithm can reveal about sensitive data. This paper investigates its fundamental cost in online learning, comparing learning without privacy, with pure differential privacy, and with approximate differential privacy. The focus is on what can be learned and whether the total number of prediction mistakes can remain finite.

The authors construct a hypothesis class that is learnable with approximate privacy but not with pure privacy when facing an adaptive adversary. This establishes a setting in which the choice of privacy definition changes learnability itself. Approximate privacy is therefore needed to obtain the demonstrated capability against adaptive behavior.

A second result shows that private online learners must make infinitely many mistakes for almost all hypothesis classes. Without privacy, an online-learnable class admits a finite mistake bound. This creates a strong separation between private and non-private learning on that criterion. Together, the results identify structural limits of privacy-constrained online learning, rather than merely a performance gap between particular algorithms.
neurips-2024-the-limits-of-differential-.tldr: The paper separates pure, approximate, and non-private online learning through learnability and finite-mistake impossibility results.

paragraphs: Combining RGB and thermal video offers opportunities for semantic segmentation under difficult lighting, including darkness and overexposure. Progress is constrained by scarce datasets and the effort required to label video densely. This paper addresses both issues through a new aerial benchmark and a semi-supervised learning baseline.

The MVUAV dataset provides an oblique bird’s-eye perspective captured by unmanned aerial vehicles. It complements existing eye-level data, covers varied daytime and nighttime conditions, and includes more than 30 semantic categories. The benchmark expands the viewpoints and lighting conditions available for studying multispectral video segmentation.

The proposed SemiMV baseline uses sparse labels together with additional unlabeled RGB-thermal videos. It combines a Cross-collaborative Consistency Learning module with denoised temporal aggregation, bringing consistency regularization and information across time into training. Evaluations on both MVSeg and MVUAV demonstrate the baseline’s effectiveness. The paired contributions provide a broader evaluation setting and a method designed to make use of the limited annotations characteristic of this task.
neurips-2024-unleashing-multispectral-vi.tldr: MVUAV adds aerial RGB-thermal video data, while SemiMV uses sparse labels and unlabeled videos for effective multispectral segmentation.

paragraphs: Text-to-video systems depend heavily on the prompts users provide, making real prompting behavior an important subject for research. This paper introduces VidProM, a dataset containing 1.67 million unique prompts from real users and 6.69 million videos generated by four diffusion models. It brings prompts and generated outputs together at a scale intended to support systematic study.

The authors describe the costly and time-consuming curation process and examine how VidProM differs from DiffusionDB, an image-generation prompt-gallery dataset. That comparison motivates a resource specifically for video generation: an existing image-prompt collection does not provide the same evidence about the text-to-video setting.

The paper proposes several research uses, including prompt engineering, more efficient video generation, and video copy detection. These are opportunities enabled by the resource, rather than reported solutions to those tasks. The dataset and related code are publicly released under a CC-BY-NC 4.0 license. The main contribution is an extensive collection of real prompts and generated videos for future investigation.
neurips-2024-vidprom-a-million-scale-rea.tldr: VidProM pairs 1.67 million real-user video prompts with 6.69 million generated videos to support research on text-to-video systems.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a teacher model to a student. A common objective uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to compare their output probabilities category by category. This paper argues that the comparison misses relationships across categories and also has difficulties with non-overlapping distributions and geometry when applied to intermediate features.

The authors introduce two methods based on Wasserstein distance. WKD-L uses discrete Wasserstein distance for logit distillation, allowing probabilities to be compared across categories and explicitly incorporating category relationships. WKD-F models feature distributions parametrically and uses continuous Wasserstein distance to transfer information from intermediate layers.

The two methods address different locations of knowledge transfer while sharing a distribution-comparison approach that accounts for structure beyond corresponding categories. Evaluations on image classification and object detection find that WKD-L outperforms strong KL-divergence variants. WKD-F also exceeds the evaluated KL-based counterparts and state-of-the-art competitors. These empirical findings support Wasserstein distance as a competitive foundation for both output-level and feature-level distillation in the tested tasks.
neurips-2024-wasserstein-distance-rivals.tldr: Wasserstein-based logit and feature distillation outperform strong comparison methods in image classification and object detection evaluations.

paragraphs: Comparing black-box prediction models often involves estimating a measure of predictive quality for each model and testing their difference. Even with cross-fitting and standardization, the test statistic can become degenerate when the models are equally good. Its limiting distribution then fails to provide the non-degenerate reference needed for conventional inference.

Zipper addresses this by evaluating predictiveness on two testing-data splits that overlap. A slider parameter determines how much data the splits share. The design builds on additional splitting while allowing controlled reuse of observations, connecting the construction of the evaluation samples to the behavior of the resulting test statistic.

The authors establish asymptotic normality under the equal-goodness null hypothesis for any fixed slider value. This supports asymptotic control of false rejection rates while effective data reuse improves power. Finite-sample experiments show that a simple slider choice works well across varied settings. The contribution offers a practical inference device for model comparisons relevant to specification testing, model selection, and assessments of variable importance.
neurips-2024-zipper-addressing-degenerac.tldr: Zipper uses overlapping evaluation splits to avoid degenerate model-comparison statistics and support valid asymptotic testing with effective data reuse.
